opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's changed quite a lot. When I was younger, especially during my PhD and the first few years after, I was pretty reluctant to do this kind of thing. I felt that as a researcher, your work should speak for itself. You write the paper, you release the code, and if it's good, people will find it. Talking about yourself in public felt a little unnecessary, maybe even a bit uncomfortable. I was also worried about saying something wrong, or something that would be taken out of context.

As I've gotten older, and especially since I started running my own lab and working with students, I've come to see it differently. A lot of what matters in research isn't captured in papers. Papers are very polished. They show the final result, but not the detours, the failed ideas, the taste, or the reasons you chose one direction over another. Those things are hard to transmit through formal channels, and conversations like this are one of the few places where you can share them.

There's also a sense of responsibility. The field is moving incredibly fast, and there's a lot of noise and a lot of hype. If people who are actually doing the research stay silent, the narrative gets shaped by others. So I feel it's worth speaking up sometimes, sharing honest views, including uncertain or unpopular ones.

I still have some hesitation. I don't want to become someone who talks more than they work. But I'm more relaxed about it now. I care less about saying everything perfectly and more about being genuine. If something I say helps a young student think about their path differently, then it's worth it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he is more relaxed and willing to share uncertain or unpopular views, but it does not attribute that change to greater willingness to risk being disliked.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question to start with, actually. Honestly, when I was younger, I avoided this kind of thing. I was a researcher, and I felt like the work should speak for itself. If the paper is good, people will read it, people will build on it, and that's the whole conversation. Going on a podcast felt almost like a distraction, or maybe a bit self-promotional, and I was uncomfortable with that.

I think two things changed. The first is just getting older and realizing that the work doesn't actually speak for itself. A paper gets read by maybe a few hundred people in the field, and even they only remember the one figure or the one number. But the reasoning behind it, why we made certain choices, what we tried that failed, what we actually believe about where the field is going, that almost never makes it into the paper. And those are often the most useful things to share, especially for students who are deciding what to work on.

The second is that the field itself changed. Ten years ago, computer vision and deep learning were a pretty niche academic community. Now everyone is paying attention, there's a lot of money, a lot of noise, and a lot of confident claims being made. I've come to feel that if people who actually do the research don't talk publicly, then the conversation gets filled by people who don't. So in a way I feel more of a responsibility now, not less.

And I'll admit I've also just become less afraid of being wrong. When you're young you want every sentence to be precise and defensible. Now I'm more comfortable saying "this is what I think today, and I might change my mind next year." That's a much more honest way to talk about research anyway, because that's how research actually works.

r001.rationale: The response says he became less afraid of being wrong and felt more responsibility to speak publicly, but it does not attribute his growing comfort to being more willing to risk being disliked.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more comfortable saying what I think, even when it’s not fully formed. When I was younger, I felt more pressure to have the right answer—to say something that would hold up to every possible criticism. That can make you reluctant to speak publicly at all.

As I’ve gotten older, I’ve become more accepting of the fact that my views will change. An interview is a conversation at a particular moment. I can explain how I’m thinking now, and later I might learn something that changes my mind. I’m more comfortable with that uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response attributes his greater comfort to accepting that his views may be incomplete or change over time. It does not say he is more willing to risk being disliked.

sol-6.1.text: I think I’ve become more comfortable saying what I actually think, including when I’m uncertain. Earlier in my career, I felt more pressure to have a polished answer—to make sure everything sounded correct before saying it publicly. As I’ve gotten older, I’ve come to appreciate that a conversation can be useful even when your thinking isn’t fully settled. You can share how you’re approaching a question without pretending you have the final answer. I still want to be careful about what I say, but I’m less worried about sounding perfect.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he is more comfortable expressing uncertain or unfinished thoughts and less worried about sounding perfect, but does not attribute this change to increased willingness to risk being disliked.
